doc.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025

chapter: Early jazz history and its reception
title: Early musicians' day jobs and Buddy Bolden's barber shop
summary: White explains most early musicians had other work, and that Bolden hung out in the barber shop run by White's relatives Nelson and Papa John Joseph.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Were you surprised along the way in your path through jazz history – I was, one time was reading a book and it mentioned one of those earlier New Orleans musicians and that they were a barber. And I think I was naïve enough to think that all those fellows, all they did was just play music. And I don’t even know if that’s possible then – it’s hard now but was it possible then?
Well you mean back in the early days of jazz?

Yeah I mean you know music for a lot of people was not a lucrative profession so I mean that’s part of the reason why you had such a big migration of musicians out of New Orleans in the teens and the twenties. But I think that most of the musicians had other professions. So the thing I think you’re referring to is that it was always said that Buddy Bolden was a barber. And thank God Don Marquis’ book proved that wrong. You know bits in jazz are like grass, they’re everywhere. But Buddy Bolden became – he was a musician more than anything else so I think he was one of the few early on but he was struggling, but he used to hang out in a barber shop. And the barber shop was on the corner from his house and you may or may not have read, I don't know if this is a set-up, but you may not have read that the barber shop where he hung out was owned and run by my relatives, Nelson Joseph and his brother John Joseph. John Joseph was Papa John Joseph, and he was one of the early jazz musicians. Because they were all musicians. Nelson played guitar, Papa John Joseph played a lot of different instruments. He was mainly a bass player but he also played clarinet and guitar and a little saxophone. He was one of the first saxophone players in jazz and played in brass bands. And they had a brother Willie who was a clarinetist who recorded in 1927. But Papa John ran the barber shop along with his brother, and then he had his own barber shop. Musicians used to hang out in the shop, congregate, book jobs from there, and there was a sign that said “musicians headquarters.” And so people would come or call when they were home, to book musicians for jobs: parties, picnics, funerals, parades, things like that. I talked to some of the younger musicians at the time who hung out in the shop, and they would get lessons from older musicians about playing and just listen to all the talk that musicians had. So yeah, I mean I knew some of the older musicians had professions like mattress makers, bricklayers, sheet metal workers, some of them were insurance men, you know George Lewis for a while had to work as a stevedore on the levee as a longshoreman where he got injured. Some musicians also taught music on the side you know, things like that. So many of them had other professions. Because, you know, music just didn’t pay enough to pay the bills. Competition was high, there were a lot of musicians around all the time so it was hard to really make a living playing music exclusively.
